claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has a naturally formed thin, adherent native iron oxide film.
The native iron oxide film acts as a passive barrier on Q235 steel at room temperature.
The native oxide film suppresses room-temperature corrosion by limiting corrosive-species access to the iron substrate.
Elevated temperature generates thermal expansion and stress in the native oxide film.
Thermally induced stress causes cracking or spallation of the native oxide film.
Cracking or spallation of the oxide exposes fresh Q235 steel to the environment.
Exposure of fresh metal following oxide degradation triggers or accelerates localized corrosion.
Acid pickling can be used to remove the native oxide layer from Q235 specimens.
At room temperature, oxide-preserved specimens will have lower corrosion current density than oxide-removed specimens.
At room temperature, oxide-preserved specimens will undergo less corrosion-related weight loss than oxide-removed specimens.
At approximately 70°C, oxide-preserved specimens will exhibit observable oxide degradation.
At approximately 70°C, oxide-preserved specimens will exhibit more localized corrosion than at room temperature.
The temperature-induced change in corrosion will be less pronounced for oxide-removed specimens because they are already unprotected.
Comparing oxide-preserved and oxide-removed Q235 specimens in 3.5% NaCl at room temperature and approximately 70°C can test whether the native oxide governs corrosion onset or suppression.
EIS, OCP, potentiodynamic polarization, weight loss, and microscopy can measure film stability and corrosion behavior in the proposed experiment.
The proposed mechanism is limited to Q235 steel bearing its storage- or pre-exposure-formed native oxide and may not apply to other alloy chemistries or deliberately modified surfaces.
